stories.title_zh: Greg Goodman坚守阵地，AI交易日趋艰难
stories.content:
Two years ago, Greg Goodman said a pivot from huge warehouses to data centres supporting the AI boom would be a “step change” for the business he founded in 1989.

It was a big bet – for his Goodman Group, the best in industrial property globally and Australia’s largest property company, and for Greg Goodman himself, who has pinned his reputation to the pivot.

stories.title: Abang Jo on how clean energy will draw tech investments
stories.summary: Sarawak Premier Tan Sri Abang Johari Tun Openg is looking beyond Malaysian shores and politics. He is mapping out strategies to make Sarawak an investment destination for technology-intensive industries.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Abang Jo谈清洁能源将如何吸引科技投资
stories.content:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on November 2, 2026 - November 8, 2026

During *The Edge*’s first interview with Tan Sri Abang Johari Tun Openg at Wisma Bapa in March 2023, he explained why Sarawak’s state leader is called premier and not chief minister or menteri besar as in the peninsula.

The conversation then mostly revolved around the MA63 (the Malaysia Agreement 1963), the debate on rights to Sarawak’s rich hydrocarbon reserves and the state’s healthcare and education autonomy.

He told us that Sarawak recognises the Unified Examination Certificate (UEC), wanting graduates from Chinese schools to join the civil service in order to stop the brain drain. And he made it known that the state wanted to have a seaport, an international airport in Kuching (for connectivity) and an equity stake in a commercial bank (for investment capital), among others.

Three years on, Sarawak is the single largest shareholder of Affin Bank Bhd (KL:AFFIN), holding a 32% stake. It also has a 26.67% stake in Bintulu Port Holdings Bhd (KL:BIPORT), whose wholly owned subsidiary Bintulu Port Sdn Bhd was appointed the operator of the port by the Bintulu Port Authority Sarawak with all requisite approvals from the Sarawak cabinet. Hence, authority was transferred back to the state from the federal government. The state also took over MASwings and turned it into AirBorneo.

Sarawak’s gross domestic product rose to RM153.5 billion in 2025 — the fourth largest after Selangor (RM460.1 billion), Kuala Lumpur (RM265.1 billion) and Johor (RM170.9 billion), according to the Department of Statistics.

The state’s revenue grew from RM11.9 billion in 2022 to RM13.5 billion in 2025. Revenue is expected to reach RM13.6 billion this year and RM15.1 billion in 2027.

Now, the premier is looking beyond Malaysian shores and politics. He is mapping out strategies to make Sarawak an investment destination for technology-intensive industries.

The Petronas-Petros dispute is regarded as merely a technical puzzle now. “It is a question of understanding the law”, which an independent committee has been tasked to address, Abang Johari says. He is confident the issue will be resolved by year-end based on the joint declaration that he signed with Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim last year.

No longer dwelling on grievances, Abang Johari now talks about GPU (graphics processing units), gallium nitride chips and nano-satellites. He also mentions rare earth mining, insisting that Sarawak will not export the raw mineral.

“We want to export intelligence, rather than just energy,” he tells *The Edge* in an interview conducted a week after he tabled the 2027 budget at the state assembly.

Sarawak offers affordable green power and global players bring the latest technologies with them, he says. However, he acknowledges the need for the state to cultivate talents. “So I am giving free tertiary education to all Sarawakians. We are emphasising STEM subjects. The next one will be nano-satellite.”

He has stretched the horizon from 10 years to 25 years. The Post Covid-19 Development Strategy (PCDS 2030) is only the first leg, and his plan is “at least 25 years”.

His brainchild is a 2,000ha site at Tanjung Embang that will have a low-carbon gas hub, a seaport about 8km off shore, a Doha-style transit airport built on Sarawak’s own account and an artificial intelligence (AI) grid campus.

This isn’t just a grand plan on paper. Last month, Soft Bank Group Corp, Grab Holdings Ltd and Petroleum Sarawak Bhd (Petros) entered into a framework agreement to explore developing an AI and digital infrastructure platform in Sarawak. The three parties will develop a road map for the phased development of the platform.

In September, the 76-year-old leader dropped a bomb shell, saying that this could be his “final year”. When asked about the continuity of the state’s long-term grand plans, Abang Johari replies that no one can go against nature, so he needs to groom leaders.

The Sarawak state assembly was dissolved last Monday (Oct 26). Some say that may set the stage for his successor to step up.

The following are excerpts from the interview conducted by Isabelle Francis, Jose Barrock and Kathy Fong.

*The Edge*: Premier, under your leadership, Sarawak has achieved quite a lot. For instance, greater autonomy in education and healthcare, owning a substantial stake in Affin Bank, and you have an airline now. Are you happy with what you have gotten so far, and what’s the next plan under Post Covid-19 Development Strategy 2030 (PCDS 2030)?

**Abang Johari:** The basics are still based on what we have agreed under our PCDS policy, meaning we have to give emphasis to the future for Sarawak based on her strength. Sarawak’s strength is basically in energy. Energy is the key transformation agent, from the first revolution until today, which is the fifth revolution.

And from energy, then you have to formulate policies on how to get investments in. But it must be a high-end investment strategy. When you talk about, for instance, microelectronics, we cannot be just an assembler, we must be involved at the front end, in terms of producing the tool itself.

First, I introduced what I call the digital economy \[as a means\] to leapfrog. And after that, we talk about the hydrogen economy because hydrogen is clean energy. Hydrogen, you can extract it from water and natural gas. We have abundant water resources, hydropower dams, as well as natural gas.

And from then on, you have to assemble the strategic enablers to achieve the objective.

The acquisition of a bank is a commercial transaction. At the same time, we are on the island of Borneo. We must have connectivity. So I discussed with the federal government that perhaps we take over MasWing. So it has become Air Borneo now.

And developing ports is also important. I am very pleased that the government has agreed to give us back Bintulu Port.

**Premier, you’re also going to build another seaport and a new airport?**

Yes, yes. I have identified Tanjong Embang as another industrial hub. I call it both an aeropolis as well as a new gas hub — a low-carbon gas hub. And this area is more than 2,000ha.

Another one is our international airport. And then surrounding it, we will build what we call an AI grid campus. You see, AI now is basically connected to data centres. It requires a lot of energy and water, so we have to prepare for that.

In five to seven years, there will be the AI grid. We have to prepare for that because technology advances so fast. Now you have what we call a supercomputer. The computing will enable data to flow in real time. You don’t have to store data. The data will flow as long as you have very strong connectivity.

**Is it fibre optic (connectivity)?**

Not necessarily fibre (optic).

Cloud computing will be the key. When you have the flow of data at the speed of light, what you need is just the GPU (graphics processing unit). I went to Bristol in the UK. I saw a lab researching this. That’s why in IT, the next phase will be supercomputers. And then the result of that \[is\] what I call, AI grid. Actually, Europe has already started \[on this\].

**When do you plan to start work on the AI grid campus?**

Next year, January … the moment \[the Sarawak state\] budget is passed. Completion should be soon. It will fast track development by our state agencies. Of course, it is public-private partnership.

The Asian Development Bank in Manila asked us about this development because they are very interested.

**So for the AI hubs, when will we see it happen?**

I have a meeting on it after this. The developer \[of the AI Grid campus\] is Petros (Petroleum Sarawak Bhd). The whole area includes a deep seaport. The seaport will be about 8km \[from shore\]. It’ll be built with the carbon capture \[facilities\]. And it will be linked to our Bintulu Port.

**When you say link with Bintulu Port, what does that mean?**

The shipping industry is now shifting from hydrocarbon-based fossil fuels to low-carbon fuels.

And low-carbon fuel will be methanol or ammonia. Bintulu Port will be equipped with the production of \[low-carbon fuel\] because we already have our methanol there. Then you can provide bunkering facilities to the international shipping companies that come from the West, India, \[through\] Strait of Malacca, Japan, China …

And, of course, our advantage is that we still have the space. Singapore has also approached us. It’s Bintulu Port that will manage it.

**What role will Singapore play?**

They are just talking to us on how to collaborate with them. It’s very preliminary. What we are looking into is more on the services that they can provide to the shipping industry on that route to East Asia.

But one thing, we have our own strength, we have the gas. We are producing methanol after the \[Strait of\] Hormuz problem because some industries are depending on the Middle East supply. There are inquiries from the buyers whether we can increase the production of methanol because we’ve got one \[production plant\] in Bintulu and the other one in Labuan. What we’re going to do is we have to expand, include green methanol.

**Is this low carbon hub a 10-year plan?**

Oh no, no … it has to be a longer-term plan because we are now recognised by the World Economic Forum as a new emerging industrial cluster. You know, the only one in Malaysia, because of our low-carbon \[fuel supply\]. Out of 1,339 recognised in the world, \[among\] the new ones, one is in Malaysia — Samalaju.

**So, for \[the supply of\] green energy, what are you looking at?**

Gas is still green, \[although\] they call it blue; it’s still low carbon. And then we have hydro \[power\]. And hydro is being expanded into what we call \[pumped\] storage hydropower. And also cascading dams. And we have solar power. Floating solar panels as well as solar panels on the land. And then we got biomass. We got four \[types of green energy\]. So, we have a mixture of renewable energy, and that’s why we are able to participate in what we call Asean Power Grid. We are now supplying to Kalimantan, Indonesia. And we are supplying power to Sabah. Next will be Brunei. And then after that, Singapore, Peninsular Malaysia.

**So the submarine cable is happening? And how about the funding?**

Yes, it is. The only thing is that Singapore and us (Sarawak) have to work together with Indonesia because of the \[sea\] corridor for us to lay it. There is a corridor under Asean. I leave it to the federal government. It’s a government to government \[matter\].

I think the funding will be a collaboration between Malaysia and Singapore. In Malaysia, they’re talking about TNB (Tenaga Nasional Bhd) and PETRONAS. And Sembcorp is for Singapore. For us, Sarawak, it is just producing power.

**Are you building the airport with Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB) or is it a state project?**

It’s on our own. But now there has been discussion. Apparently, MAHB is interested in taking equity. We need a state-of-the-art airport.

I have seen how Doha Airport was built. The traffic to Africa, to Europe, as well to Asia … the design is such that passengers in transit won’t lose their direction. I don’t take 100% \[of the design\], but use that as a model.

**Is there still a lot more gas to be discovered and developed in Sarawak?**

Yes. There’s one gas field outside of Kuching, the western field, except that the gas is sour gas with high sulphur and carbon dioxide. But there is technology now to separate them, and then the sour gas will become sweet gas.

And based on the preliminary study, the gas reserve is quite substantial there. You must remember the \[gas reserve\] belt. The gas reserves and oil are from the northern part of Borneo; Kimanis, then it goes down to Brunei, to Baram, goes down to Mukah, and now it’s Balingian. It’s halfway \[through Borneo\]. And then after that, they go to Natuna. So the geology is there. Now is only the question of technology.

**Premier, what we’re talking about now is old gas. But there’s a lot of new gas that has not contracted …**

Yes, we have the Adong Kecil onshore, done by Petros. And that’s only one well, 800 barrels per day. It’s supposed to be about eight wells there, onshore. And now you’ve got a new technology on exploration of gas \[onshore\].

Balangian is onshore. Let’s see how it goes.

**Premier, you shared with us in a previous interview the plan to install 10 gigawatts (GW) by 2020 and 15GW in 2035. Is that on track?**

Yes, 2030 is on track \[with\] 10GW. Then 2035, we expect we can generate 15GW based on our development in solar, and you must also take into consideration the development of batteries \[technology\], because solar \[power\] depends on batteries. And then the new technology replaces lithium with sodium now.

Now they are saying, instead of four hours, the battery can supply 12 hours. At the moment, we are producing 50MW from Batang Ai (hydroelectric plant).

We are working with China. Number two is Masdar Abu Dhabi (Future Energy Company). And then there is one more \[party\] doing a study on our Murum Dam, Baleh Dam and Bakun Dam.

**Premier, all these plans, but then you say you might step down.**

Oh (laughs). Basically, I’m talking about age. You cannot go against nature. But we have the basics now, then we have to groom \[the next\] leadership to continue \[with developments\]. Because this one (AI grid campus) is not a 10-year plan. It could be 20 years. The direction is already there. What is also important is inclusivity and political stability. Now we are talking about the export of intelligence with energy \[that we have\].

Petros is now talking to SoftBank (Group Corp) and Grab Holdings Ltd.

That’s why I am preparing our human resources by giving free education. I am giving free tertiary education to all Sarawakians. So we are emphasising on STEM subjects.

The next one will be nano-satellite. I’m going into satellite also because the next trend is data intelligence — data and semiconductors going together. And Malaysia must be able to design semiconductors, design chips. And we are doing it now because we are supplying chips, even to China.

If you look at the semiconductor industry, Nvidia Corp is very strong in design. And then Taiwan’s TSMC is producing it. For us, we have our own foundry now, X-Fab; it’s been there more than 10 years. What we need now is a new semiconductor chip that can keep the volume of data. It has to be a new chip, a gallium nitride chip. At the moment, it’s silicon. But silicon chips cannot store a volume of data because when you store \[a large volume of\] data, it produces heat. If you are using silicon chips that cannot contain the heat, then *habis lah*.

I think Malaysia can do it. Sarawak can do it. We have tried. Our work is at a lab in Cardiff, the UK. Now we have produced it. They call it K-E-T-E-Q AI. Our chip is used by China for their electric meters. The chip is designed by Sarawakians.

**Does that mean Sarawak already has a supply chain for the semiconductor industry?**

More or less. That’s why we have to produce a new generation of chips, which will link to our nano-satellite. For a space economy, you must have your own satellite to keep your data, and at the same time, to detect new data.

And you must have a constellation of satellites. That’s why you go for a nano-satellite in low orbit. If you go for a higher one, it’s very costly. But what is important is that you can extract data from Earth.

Our university has a faculty now in space \[science\]. The Sarawak Space Agency now is chaired by former Chief of Defence Forces Tan Sri Affendi Buang. I studied the case of Measat. The ground station was not that well prepared. We have even studied RazakSat. What is important now is having a strong ground station capable of communicating with low-Earth-orbit satellites. If you want to go towards exporting intelligence, you must have all these ecosystems.

**You’re looking at the satellite business as well?**

Yes. \[At the moment\] I’m just studying what happened to Measat. And then we will analyse where the weaknesses are. Because our advantage is our location right on the equator.

So, you have an advantage with your satellites out there, low orbit. Then you must have a group of satellites. The communication must be consistent. For this, I have to work with the federal government. I told them, because your data is important, it’s sovereign data.

**You mentioned political stability just now. How do you find the current situation in Malaysia?**

I can’t talk about Peninsular. As far as Sarawak is concerned, we manage to have stability.

**How’s your relationship with the federal government?**

Cordial. We have worked with every prime minister. After (Datuk Seri) Najib Razak, then (Tun) Dr Mahathir Mohamad. After that (Tan Sri) Muhiyiddin Yassin and (Datuk Seri) Ismail Sabri Yaakob.

**Has Umno approached you about the passing of the national budget?**

Some people did ask for my view, but I said I’m concentrating on our state budget.

**Under the Pakatan Harapan leadership, has it been better for Sarawak? If Umno comes back, do you think it would be different?**

No, no, it’s up to them. But the ultimate is for Malaysia’s stability. You know, when I was called by the \[previous\] Agong (Sultan of Pahang, Al-Sultan Abdullah Ri’ayatuddin Al-Mustafa Billah Shah), the last time, His Majesty asked ‘Are you willing to join the unity government?’ Then I replied to the Agong, *menjunjung titah demi untuk Malaysia* (accepting the King’s order for the country).

Stability is very important. You know, we (Malaysia) were quite far ahead of Vietnam at one time. We were ahead of even South Korea. But now we are behind them. And all our neighbours are prospering. Malaysia has the strength. It is a question of how you manage it.

**Sarawak’s potential to create plenty of energy, green power. Instead of exporting energy, the state wants to export intelligence. How is this concept different from the past?**

This is the reason why I want to establish the AI grid campus, so all activities will be there, because all these — like storage of data, dissemination of data and transport of data intelligence — all require power. So, we establish the AI grid campus because we have energy to offer and then let the global players come here and that will create jobs for our people.

But we must have talents \[to attract investments\]. That’s why we have talent development through our universities. So that there will be high-pay jobs \[available\]. Our strength is having power, \[while\] investors’ strengths are knowledge and technologies. They come in with the ‘brains’; and then (we) export intelligence, backed by our graduates who will be under the top management. For all you know, our people can create something new.

Costs will be a main concern for investors. If your \[price of\] power is reasonable, why won’t they come here? Whoever can provide me better terms, I will go there. But what the locals should do is ramp up their intelligence and also build the ecosystem.

That’s why I give free education. It cost me RM200 million for the first cohort. The second cohort will be another RM200 million. The third year, another RM200 million. At least, I have to allocate RM1 billion.

We then produce 10,000 \[graduates\] a year, graduates of high calibre in 64 disciplines, all science-based. Only a few in finance, banking, psychology and cybersecurity. Swinburne, Curtin, University of Technology Sarawak and also iCATS University College — they are the ones supplying \[human capital\]. Then, we sponsor them \[the graduates\] to do master’s programmes overseas.

The new area \[of study\] is the seven elements of rare earth.…

stories.title: Microsoft ends AI infrastructure deal with Oracle amid re-evaluation
stories.summary: Microsoft is discontinuing its artificial intelligence (AI) computing partnership with Oracle Corp, opting not to renew a 2023 agreement. This decision is part of Microsoft's broader review of external cloud computing commitments and its data center infrastructure strategy.
stories.title_zh: Microsoft在重新评估后终止与Oracle的AI基础设施协议
stories.content:
Microsoft is phasing out an artificial intelligence (AI) computing partnership with Oracle Corp, choosing not to renew a 2023 agreement, Bloomberg has reported.The company has steadily deactivated rented server capacity from Oracle in recent months. These Oracle-hosted machines used older generations of Nvidia Corp. chips, which no longer meet Microsoft's current computing requirements.The shift underscores growing industry concerns regarding hardware obsolescence. Research firm Gartner Inc. has cautioned that aggressive capital expenditures on AI infrastructure risk significant write-downs as faster, more efficient chips enter the market.For Oracle, the loss of capacity utilization exacerbates existing challenges. Substantial capital outlays for AI data center construction have driven its free cash flow into negative territory, pushing its credit rating to just one level above junk status.Neither company disclosed the financial value of the 2023 contract, which was intended to support Microsoft’s AI-powered Bing search engine. This wind-down follows an earlier Business Insider report indicating that separate negotiations to lease additional Oracle capacity failed in June this year.Microsoft is actively reviewing over $80 billion in outside cloud computing commitments from various providers, including CoreWeave, Nscale, and Nebius Group. Company executives are reportedly dissatisfied with escalating expenses and operational delays associated with these third-party agreements.The tech giant recently declined an option to expand an Nscale deployment in Texas, a deal that could have been worth tens of billions of dollars. This decision came weeks after Microsoft withdrew from a planned Nscale site in Loughton, Essex, due to power connection delays that pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s.

- AI & Compute Infrastructure
- 1 min Read

# Microsoft ends AI infrastructure deal with Oracle amid re-evaluation

Microsoft is discontinuing its artificial intelligence (AI) computing partnership with Oracle Corp, opting not to renew a 2023 agreement. This decision is part of Microsoft's broader review of external cloud computing commitments and its data center infrastructure strategy.

- Published On Nov 07, 2026 at 11:20 AM IST

## Highlights

- Microsoft is ending its AI computing partnership with Oracle, not renewing a 2023 agreement.
- Rented Oracle server capacity with older Nvidia chips no longer aligns with Microsoft's needs.
- Microsoft is reviewing over $80 billion in external cloud commitments with various providers.
- The company declined Nscale expansions in Texas and withdrew from a UK site due to delays.

## Comments

What are your thoughts?

stories.title: Data centre power market set to hit USD $107 billion
stories.summary: Rising AI power demand and grid delays are pushing operators to upgrade electrical systems as the market is forecast to reach USD $107.06 billion by 2034.
stories.title_zh: 数据中心 power market 预计将达到 1070 亿美元
stories.content:
Polaris Market Research projects the data centre power and energy management market will reach USD $107.06 billion by 2034, up from USD $35.95 billion in 2025.

That implies a compound annual growth rate of 12.9% as operators invest more in power infrastructure for facilities running artificial intelligence workloads and other dense computing systems. The research highlights electricity supply, power distribution and energy monitoring as central issues for data centre developers as rack power ratings rise and grid connection delays hold up new projects.

Power systems once treated as supporting infrastructure are moving closer to the centre of investment decisions. Operators are replacing older electrical equipment with intelligent power distribution units, higher-capacity uninterruptible power supply systems and advanced switchgear. Rack-level monitoring is also becoming more common as workloads grow more power intensive.

The study identifies energy generation as the fastest-growing solution segment, with annual growth of 13.5% projected through 2034. That reflects a shift towards gas generator sets, solar installations, fuel cells and batteries as operators seek ways to bring new capacity online before utility connections are available.

Regulation is also shaping demand. In Europe, efficiency reporting has added pressure on operators to measure and improve facility performance, while public comparisons of metrics such as power usage effectiveness are likely to influence investment choices.

### Operator demand

Hyperscale operators accounted for the largest share of the market in 2025, at 37.33%. The research says these companies are increasingly setting power architecture, onsite generation and monitoring requirements at the design stage rather than adding them after a facility is built.

Colocation providers face different incentives because they sell power capacity to tenants. In that model, rack-level metering and phased additions of protected capacity can directly affect revenue, while modular UPS systems let operators expand within existing halls instead of building new space. Spending by colocation providers is projected to rise at an annual rate of 12.7%.

Software is emerging as a significant part of the market alongside physical equipment. Predictive analytics, digital twins and AI-led controls are being used to estimate future power needs, support upgrade planning and adjust backup systems to free unused capacity.

The market still faces barriers. Advanced power systems require significant upfront spending, and retrofitting live data centres can be difficult because operators must integrate new equipment with legacy infrastructure while maintaining uptime. Connected electrical equipment also increases cybersecurity risks, which may slow adoption among smaller enterprise operators.

### Regional split

North America held the largest regional share in 2025 at 38.58%, equivalent to about USD $13.87 billion. The research cites US Department of Energy estimates that data centres could consume 649 TWh by 2030, or about 11.8% of US electricity, underlining the scale of the region's demand challenge.

Europe is expected to grow at 12.3% annually, with the regional market projected to reach USD $27.7 billion by 2034. Efficiency rules and grid constraints are pushing colocation providers towards smart power systems, storage and renewable energy.

Asia Pacific is forecast to record the fastest growth, at 14.6%, reaching USD $30.2 billion by 2034. Expansion in China, India, Japan and Australia is driving the increase as operators add data centre capacity across the region.

In the Middle East and Africa, projected growth stands at 13.6%, supported by demand for efficient equipment in hot climates and interest in solar energy. Grid reliability issues in parts of Africa are also increasing the value of backup and onsite power. Latin America is expected to grow at 13.4%, combining strong renewable energy resources with rising hyperscale demand.

### Competitive moves

The market is also seeing consolidation and product development as suppliers try to broaden their reach across power equipment, cooling and control systems. Schneider Electric has worked with AMD on a reference design for racks of up to 246 kW and has introduced software-defined medium-voltage switchgear. ABB has launched a direct current portfolio for artificial intelligence facilities.

Recent deals point in the same direction. Eaton bought Boyd Thermal for USD $9.5 billion to combine liquid cooling with power systems, while Vertiv agreed to acquire UtilityInnovation Group for about USD $1.45 billion to expand its microgrid controls and behind-the-meter offering. Generac is also buying Enercon for switchgear and enclosures.

Onsite electricity supply is drawing investment as well. Bloom Energy has expanded its partnership with Oracle to up to 2.8 GW of fuel cells, with 1.2 GW contracted, while Cummins has announced what it described as its largest battery storage system for a US data centre.

The research suggests technologies including high-voltage direct current distribution, battery storage and microgrid controls are moving from trial deployments towards broader commercial use as operators look for faster and more flexible ways to secure electricity for new capacity.

US Department of Energy scenarios cited in the research place data centres at between 9.5% and 15.3% of US electricity demand by 2030.

stories.title: Data centre sector 'politically salient'; Singapore takes practical approach to regulation: Tan Kiat How
stories.summary: Senior minister Tan Kiat How emphasized that Singapore pursues selective data center growth aligned with national economic priorities rather than unconditional capacity maximization. The pragmatic regulatory stance aims to attract high-value AI and financial services workloads while managing the city-state's severe land and carbon constraints.
stories.why_it_matters: Singapore's calibrated approach creates a two-tier market: premium operators with sustainability credentials and government relationships gain protected access, while speculative or less efficient projects face exclusion. This policy clarity reduces regulatory uncertainty for targeted investors but increases competitive pressure to demonstrate carbon efficiency and economic value-add. For regional competitors like Malaysia and Indonesia, Singapore's selectivity represents a deliberate release valve that channels overflow demand their way—if they can build fast enough and solve their own infrastructure constraints.

stories.title_zh: 数据中心行业"具有政治敏感性"；新加坡采取务实监管方式：Tan Kiat How
stories.summary_zh: 高级部长Tan Kiat How强调，新加坡追求与国家经济优先事项相一致的selective数据中心增长，而非无条件的容量最大化。这一务实的监管立场旨在吸引高价值AI和金融服务工作负载，同时管理这个城邦严重的土地和碳约束。
stories.why_zh: 新加坡的精细调控方法创造了一个双层市场：拥有可持续发展资质和政府关系的优质运营商获得受保护的准入，而投机性或效率较低的项目面临排除。这一政策清晰度减少了目标投资者的监管不确定性，但增加了展示碳效率和经济附加值的竞争压力。对马来西亚和印尼等区域竞争对手而言，新加坡的选择性代表了一个有意设计的释放阀，将溢出需求导向它们——前提是它们能足够快地建设并解决自身基础设施约束。
stories.content:
The Republic is not out to compete ‘for every megawatt’ of capacity, aims to strengthen regional capabilities

\[SINGAPORE\] Data centres have become “politically salient”, Tan Kiat How, Singapore’s Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, said on Friday (Nov 6).

With communities and policymakers asking “legitimate questions around... water, land, grid capacity and what they receive in return”, he emphasised the need for industry and government to collaborate for sustainable growth in the sector.

His comments came in the wake of American voters’ bruising rebuke to data centre expansion in the US, as midterm election results widely seen as signalling support for restrictions on development have fuelled a global sell-off in tech stocks.

stories.title: Ongoing labor dispute sees Micron pause construction at its $4.5bn memory fab in Taoyuan, Taiwan – report
stories.summary: Micron has paused construction at its $4.5 billion memory fab in Taiwan following an on-going labor dispute.
stories.title_zh: 持续的劳资纠纷导致Micron暂停其位于台湾桃园的价值45亿美元memory fab建设——报道
stories.content:
Micron has paused construction at its $4.5 billion memory fab in Taiwan following an on-going labor dispute.

According to a report from Bloomberg, activity at the Fab 11E site in Taoyuan, northwestern Taiwan, was halted due to “mounting uncertainties,” including Micron’s concern that an agreement it struck with the Taoyuan labor union may get overturned.

The fab was originally expected to come online in 2028, with Micron having already purchased tools from ASML for the facility, the report said.

While Micron hasn’t provided a statement regarding the stoppage, Bloomberg noted the company had informed local officials and suppliers of its plan to suspend construction at the site.

The disruption follows a tense few months for Micron as it became the latest memory chip company to see its workers fight for increased compensation in the wake of record-breaking profits as a result of growing memory demands to support the AI build-out.

Unionized workers at Samsung’s South Korean facilities called off a proposed strike in May of this year after reaching an agreement with the company regarding issues over bonuses and wage increases. Meanwhile, in August of this year, SK Hynix reached a tentative agreement with workers that is set to significantly change how the memory giant’s profit-sharing bonuses will be distributed.

Last month, Micron agreed to a deal with two of its biggest unions; however, citing sources familiar with the situation, Bloomberg said Micron may have to reopen negotiations as not all employees are happy with the outcome.

However, almost 70 percent of union members at the Taoyuan site rejected the offer put forward by management, calling for clearer profit-sharing arrangements and terms for bonuses. The two sides were expected to meet again today (November 6) to further negotiate.

Micron has invested around $50bn in Taiwan over the last three decades and plans to manufacture high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and DRAM chips at the Taoyuan fab. The country currently accounts for around 60 percent of the company’s global DRAM output and the majority of its HBM production.

In January 2026, Micron signed a Letter of Intent (LOI) to acquire Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation’s (PSMC) P5 fabrication site in Tongluo, Taiwan, for $1.8bn. At the time, the company said the agreement would see it take ownership and control of the P5 site, allowing it to increase DRAM production in phases and meet long-term demand from its customers.

Memory companies have warned that the memory chip shortage is likely to persist into 2027 and beyond, with consumer electronics the most likely to suffer in the face of ongoing shortages, as capacity will increasingly become allocated to AI infrastructure projects.

In January 2025, the Wall Street Journal reported that data from TrendForce shows that up to 70 percent of the memory produced worldwide in 2026 will be consumed by data centers.

stories.title: NTT Data signs 900MW fuel cell supply deal with Bloom Energy
stories.summary: Japanese technology firm NTT Data has signed a 900MW deployment agreement with fuel cell company Bloom Energy to deploy fuel cells across multiple data center projects worldwide.
stories.title_zh: NTT Data与Bloom Energy签署900MW fuel cell供应协议
stories.content:
Japanese technology firm NTT Data has signed a 900MW deployment agreement with fuel cell company Bloom Energy to deploy fuel cells across multiple data center projects worldwide.

Under the terms of the agreement, Bloom will supply NTT with its solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) systems, which will be deployed on-site to power the company’s data centers. The partners said that initial shipments of the fuel cell generators are expected to start in 2027.

According to its website, NTT Data Group operates more than 150 data centers in more than 20 countries and regions. In Japan, the company operates data centers in Tokyo (TKY11) and Osaka (OSK11 and OSK12). In October, it was reported that the company was in talks to develop a $6.3 billion data center in Western Japan for Anthropic.

“Our clients are building AI capabilities at a pace the grid alone cannot always match, and speed to power has become one of the defining factors in delivering capacity when and where it’s needed,” said Doug Adams, CEO of NTT Global Data Centers. “Bloom’s onsite power gives us a reliable, scalable way to bring capacity online alongside construction, while honoring our commitment to the communities where we build and operate. Its fuel cells protect local air quality, use minimal water, and run quietly, which matters to us just as much as the megawatts. This agreement gives us a foundation to power our clients’ growth across our global portfolio.”

Bloom is a developer of SOFC generators, dubbed the Bloom Box, which are stationary power generators that convert fuels into electricity through an electrochemical process without combustion. While they can be powered via hydrogen, at present the vast majority rely on natural gas. The deal with NTT represents the firm's largest deal with a single data center developer.

“Companies that can secure power quickly will have a differentiated advantage and accelerated path to revenue,” added Aman Joshi, EVP and chief commercial officer at Bloom Energy. “As AI compute makes its way from AI factories to deployment at scale for edge and inference use cases, we at Bloom are uniquely positioned to help our customers meet the moment by enabling time to power with highly reliable, cleaner power that meets AI workload requirements for the digital era.”

Bloom has signed a range of deals across the data center spectrum over recent years.

Earlier this year, it expanded an agreement with cloud firm Oracle to supply it with up to 2.8GW of capacity. The companies inked a deal last year for an initial 1.2GW of capacity. However, deployments of the technology at Oracle’s Jupiter data center in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, have faced roadblocks due to opposition to the extension of a gas pipeline expected to feed the facility's fuel cells.

Bloom has also signed deals with Equinix for deployments across 19 data centers with a capacity exceeding 100MW, as well as an agreement with US utility American Electric Power for up to 1GW of SOFCs to power AI data centers off-grid. In October, AEP signed a 20-year Power Purchase Agreement with Google, which committed to offtake 702MW of power from a fuel cell generation project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, which utilizes Bloom’s fuel cells.

stories.title: Global AI sell-off wipes RM4.46 bil off Bursa's 20 largest tech stocks
stories.summary: Bursa Malaysia’s 20 largest technology stocks shed over RM4.46 billion in market value on Friday as a global sell-off in artificial intelligence (AI)-related counters spread to the country’s chipmakers and equipment suppliers.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 全球AI抛售抹去马来西亚交易所20大科技股44.6亿令吉市值
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 6): Bursa Malaysia’s 20 largest technology stocks shed over RM4.46 billion in market value on Friday as a global sell-off in artificial intelligence (AI)-related counters spread to the country’s chipmakers and equipment suppliers.

The Bursa Malaysia Technology Index, which tracks 54 counters, fell 3.26 points or 4.58% to 67.88, the steepest decline among Bursa’s sector indices. The country's benchmark FBM KLCI shed 19.28 points to close at 1,616.58 after touching an intraday low of 1,610.8.

The heavy selldown, which extended into a second day on Friday, followed growing concerns among investors over whether earnings from major AI and technology companies could justify the billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure. The Democrats’ strong showing in the US midterm elections also added to concerns that closer scrutiny of data centres could slow investment.

Affin Pheim Asset Management fund manager Khoo Zing Sheng said the Trump administration’s determination to preserve the US lead over China could leave room for compromise on AI policy.

“In the short term, I see this as a necessary, volatile repricing rather than a quick ‘buy-the-dip’ moment,” he told *The Edge.*

ViTrox Corp Bhd (KL:VITROX), the largest stock in the local technology index, accounted for RM909.55 million of the loss on Friday. Shares in the automated test equipment maker fell 4.53% to RM10.12 — its biggest single-day fall since March 2026 — despite reporting its strongest quarterly earnings since its listing in 2005 just a day earlier.

Chip assembly and testing companies Inari Amertron Bhd (KL:INARI) and Malaysian Pacific Industries Bhd (KL:MPI) also came under selling pressure, losing a combined RM1.15 billion in market value.

Inari extended Thursday's losses, falling 7.02% to RM2.12, while MPI shed 6.89% to RM36.20 — marking its biggest single-day loss since May 2025.

Among the 20 heavyweights, factory automation specialist Greatech Technology Bhd (KL:GREATEC) recorded the steepest percentage decline, falling 7.69% to RM2.40. The four companies together accounted for RM2.57 billion, or nearly 58%, of the total loss in market value.

Of the 20 stocks, 18 fell and two closed unchanged. Despite Friday’s losses, 14 of the 18 decliners remained in positive territory year-to-date, with ViTrox still up 154% for the year.

The Bursa Malaysia Technology Index ended Friday about 15.5% below its multi-year peak of 80.32, but 34.3% above its March 30 low of 50.56.

“We would view the current weakness as a potential valuation reset rather than a broad-based deterioration in industry fundamentals,” Berjaya Research Sdn Bhd head of research Kenneth Leong said.

The selling over the past two sessions largely reflected a reassessment of valuations and growth expectations, he added.

Edited ByEmir Zainul

stories.title: Nvidia boosts chip tracking in Southeast Asia to fight smuggling
stories.summary: Nvidia is implementing enhanced tracking mechanisms including serial number monitoring and end-user verification for AI accelerators distributed across Southeast Asia. The crackdown responds to US government pressure and evidence that substantial chip volumes were being diverted to Chinese entities through regional transshipment channels.
stories.why_it_matters: Enhanced tracking transforms Nvidia's commercial relationships in Southeast Asia from simple vendor transactions into compliance partnerships with significant legal exposure. Distributors and system integrators face new operational burdens and potential liability, which may consolidate market share toward larger, more compliance-capable partners and raise costs for legitimate buyers. For Southeast Asian governments, the policy tension between attracting AI investment and avoiding US secondary sanctions complicates industrial strategy, particularly for Singapore and Malaysia positioning as neutral technology hubs.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Nvidia加强Southeast Asia芯片追踪以打击走私
stories.summary_zh: Nvidia正在对分布于东南亚的AI加速器实施增强追踪机制，包括序列号监控和最终用户验证。这一打击行动回应了美国政府压力以及大量芯片通过区域转运渠道被转往中国实体的证据。
stories.why_zh: 增强追踪将Nvidia在东南亚的商业关系从简单的供应商交易转变为具有重大法律风险的合规合作伙伴关系。分销商和系统集成商面临新的运营负担和潜在责任，这可能使市场份额向更大、更具合规能力的合作伙伴集中，并提高合法买家的成本。对东南亚政府而言，吸引AI投资与避免美国二级制裁之间的政策张力使工业战略复杂化，特别是对定位为中立技术枢纽的新加坡和马来西亚。
stories.content:
(Nov 6): Nvidia Corp is stepping up monitoring of artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators sold in Southeast Asia, a strategic step to curtail semiconductor smuggling after criticism it hasn’t done enough to stop shipments from illegally reaching Chinese companies.

The chipmaker now requires customers in the region to enrol in its so-called fleet intelligence system — which tracks the location of AI accelerators owned by participating companies, among other metrics — in order to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners, or NCPs, according to people familiar with the matter.

The NCP designation is highly coveted for AI cloud computing providers, granting both a public stamp of approval and preferred chip access from a company that plays kingmaker to the industry. Nvidia’s idea is to use the carrot of that label to encourage broader uptake of what remains a voluntary chip tracking programme, said the people, who requested anonymity to discuss a confidential new measure.

That could provide more visibility into how Nvidia hardware moves through a region that’s long been a transshipment point for restricted goods. The US government broadly prohibits Chinese companies from purchasing advanced Nvidia AI chips without a licence, though authorities believe firms there have nonetheless gotten their hands on billions of dollars’ worth of the hardware, primarily via smuggling networks in Southeast Asia.

As cases mount, Nvidia and some US authorities have sparred over who is responsible for solving the problem. Corners of Washington are frustrated that the chipmaker has repeatedly missed red flags, while Nvidia has shot back that it follows laws as written — putting the onus on government officials to identify bad actors. Those officials, meanwhile, disagree on the appropriate tack for their own response, with frustration brewing in the Trump administration and on Capitol Hill.

There is no better illustration of the quagmire than Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, which has been under US and Singapore investigation for more than a year and returned to the limelight last week after *The New York Times* reported that Washington suspects one of the company’s top executives of spying for Beijing, leveraging her close relationship with Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

In response, Huang said his interactions with Megaspeed were “completely normal”, while an Nvidia spokesperson said the chipmaker is “confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know”. That aligns with Nvidia’s posture on earlier chip diversion suspicions; the chipmaker said last year that it asked the US government whether it needed to alter its relationship with Megaspeed, and was told no. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

Nvidia’s response hasn’t satisfied Capitol Hill, where key House Republicans this week requested a briefing from the CEO.

The status of Nvidia’s own due diligence on Megaspeed — concerning the smuggling suspicions, rather than espionage — is also unclear. Huang said last week that “we’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one”, referring to graphics processing units. That goes a step beyond previous statements on the matter from Nvidia, which said last year — after getting pressed about discrepancies in Megaspeed’s data centre footprint — that it had identified “substantially” all the products sent to the company.

Nvidia also pledged in December 2025 to visit Megaspeed’s data centres again in the near future, but since then has repeatedly declined to say whether such checks have occurred. That’s even after Megaspeed’s main computing hub landlord dropped it as a tenant and two other data centre operators in Southeast Asia disputed Nvidia’s account of the location of Megaspeed’s chips. Asked again this week whether Nvidia had conducted any additional checks that would support its CEO’s assertions about counting “every” processor, a spokesperson declined to comment.

In the meantime, however, Nvidia has begun flirting with self-regulation. The biggest such example is fleet intelligence — first debuted nearly a year ago, after the US began prosecuting alleged chip smugglers and Washington’s suspicions about Megaspeed became public. It’s primarily a data centre management tool, collecting a range of information about deployments of Nvidia hardware that’s useful for operators. By also gathering geolocation information for individual parts, though, it doubles as a response to US diversion concerns.

The product underscores both that Nvidia has the tools to geolocate its chips and that it remains cautious about using them. For one, fleet intelligence does not by default require participants to share location data with Nvidia or the US government. An Nvidia spokesperson previously told *Bloomberg* that should Washington regulators want information from the database, they would communicate directly with users, without elaborating further.

A big question for the latest update, related to NCP designations, is whether Nvidia may ultimately require existing NCPs — such as Megaspeed, which won the label within a week of its 2023 creation — to sign up to maintain their privileged status. Nvidia declined to comment on this question or answer others for this story, including whether the new NCP requirement would be applied in regions beyond Southeast Asia.

Outside of fleet intelligence, Nvidia has taken several other steps to limit Chinese companies’ access to its hardware. In the wake of the biggest chip smuggling indictment in the US, the company earlier this year removed half of the Asian firms it had pre-approved for chip purchases, *Bloomberg* has reported.

More recently, it began telling buyers not to rent more than half of their Nvidia computing power to Chinese companies — even though Washington generally allows Chinese firms to use accelerators owned by others overseas. “Longstanding US policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can,” an Nvidia spokesperson told *The Financial Times*, which first reported that move. The spokesperson didn’t explain the reasoning behind the new Nvidia measure.

*Uploaded by Chng Shear Lane*

stories.title: Seremban Engineering wins RM18.21m cross-border supply chain service contract
stories.summary: Seremban Engineering Bhd’s (KL:SEB) unit has secured a cross-border supply chain services contract worth up to RMB30 million (RM18.21 million) to supply materials and equipment for data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure projects in Malaysia.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Seremban Engineering赢得1821万令吉跨境供应链服务合同
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 6): Seremban Engineering Bhd’s (KL:SEB) unit has secured a cross-border supply chain services contract worth up to RMB30 million (RM18.21 million) to supply materials and equipment for data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure projects in Malaysia.

In a Bursa Malaysia filing, Seremban Engineering, which makes process equipment and metal structures, said its wholly owned subsidiary MIE Material Resources Sdn Bhd (MMR) has entered into a cross-border supply chain service framework agreement with EPG Engineering System Sdn Bhd (EPGES).

Seremban Engineering said EPGES is a wholly owned subsidiary of a new Singapore-based customer, which is in the engineering and technical consulting industry, focusing on data centre and AI infrastructure.

Under the 12-month agreement, MMR will provide cross-border transportation from China to Malaysia, export and import customs clearance, as well as local delivery of materials, equipment and other goods from China for EPGES' projects and operations in Malaysia.

The contract runs from Nov 6, 2026 until Nov 5, 2027.

At Friday’s market close, Seremban Engineering’s share price closed unchanged at 70 sen, valuing the group at RM56 million.

Edited BySyed Azahedi

stories.title: Energy capacity struggles to keep pace with Malaysia's data centre ambitions
stories.summary: Industry specialists warn that Malaysia's electricity grid expansion timelines lag significantly behind data center construction cycles, creating a structural mismatch between announced capacity and deliverable power. The gap threatens to delay project completions and force operators toward costly on-site generation or alternative locations.
stories.why_it_matters: Malaysia's data center boom risks stalling on its own success if power cannot materialize on schedule. Developers who pre-leased capacity based on grid connection promises may face penalty clauses or customer attrition, while the country's credibility as a regional hub depends on solving this coordination failure. The pressure could accelerate regulatory reforms around power purchase agreements and distributed generation, or alternatively redirect investment flows to markets with more reliable energy timelines like Thailand or Indonesia.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 能源产能难以跟上马来西亚data centre雄心
stories.summary_zh: 行业专家警告，马来西亚电网扩张时间表显著落后于数据中心建设周期，造成宣布容量与可交付电力之间的结构性错配。这一差距可能威胁项目完工进度，并迫使运营商转向昂贵的现场发电或替代地点。
stories.why_zh: 马来西亚的数据中心繁荣若电力无法按时到位，可能因自身成功而停滞。基于电网连接承诺预先租赁容量的开发商可能面临违约条款或客户流失，而该国作为区域枢纽的信誉取决于解决这一协调失灵。压力可能加速电力购买协议和分布式发电的监管改革，或者将投资流向转向泰国或印尼等能源时间表更可靠的市场。
stories.content:
Malaysia’s push to become a regional data centre hub is putting pressure on its energy infrastructure, as new power generation and grid capacity take much longer to build than the facilities they are meant to support, according to experts.

This gap could widen as data centres take up a growing share of electricity demand, which means Malaysia needs to align its investment approvals with its plans for power generation, grid capacity and renewable energy, says Asian Strategy and Leadership Institute (ASLI) head of advisory and research advocacy Dr Fiaz Ahmad.

The challenge, he says, is making sure the infrastructure and policies behind these investments develop at the same pace as the projects themselves.

“Malaysia is not short of policy; it is short of orchestration. We have to see the connection between the opportunities and the demands that we are creating and that these data centres are bringing,” he says during a panel discussion on artificial intelligence (AI), data centres and the energy transition at CelcomDigi Responsible Business Day 2026, held at the telco’s headquarters in Petaling Jaya on Nov 5.

The sector has already drawn large sums, with Malaysia recording RM385.7 billion in data centre-related investment approvals between 2021 and the first half of 2026. Its direct contribution to gross domestic product also grew from RM0.9 billion in 2021 to RM14.1 billion in 2025, according to Bank Negara Malaysia estimates.

Fiaz says data centres are expected to make up about 21% of Malaysia’s electricity demand by 2030 and 31% by 2035, up from about 7% today. Much of this demand has yet to materialise, however, as only one of the 27 projects approved by the data centres task force is operational, he notes.

“Most of these costs and most of the benefits are still ahead of us,” he says, adding that Malaysia must plan for the infrastructure and energy needs alongside the economic opportunities, rather than treat these needs as reasons to reject data centre investments.

The other panellist, Ricardo Reina, founder of Singapore-based energy transition advisory firm Catalyze Transition, says the problem is made worse because AI infrastructure and the energy systems needed to support it are built on very different timelines.

In his presentation, Reina breaks AI infrastructure down into five layers, namely applications, AI models, computing hardware, data centre facilities and the energy system. Applications and models can be developed within months, while computing infrastructure such as graphics processing units (GPUs), servers and networking can take one to two years to set up. Data centre facilities usually take two to three years, but the energy system needs three to seven years.

“Whereas many of these data centres and facilities are being built, developed and conceptualised in a matter of two to three years, the energy system needs three to seven, even 10 years in some places, from planning to execution,” he says.

He notes that much of the grid capacity coming online today was planned in 2016, before the current wave of AI development and the resulting demand for data centres became clear.

The mismatch is most visible in the grid, Reina says, as utility companies must plan and build infrastructure years before it can be switched on, while data centre operators want to be connected much sooner. In his view, the main constraint lies in the grid rather than in the supply of power itself.

He also points out that data centres consume electricity at a steady, high level regardless of the time of day. This makes it harder to meet their demand with renewable energy, particularly solar power, which depends on sunlight.

He adds that hyperscalers, the largest cloud computing providers, are increasingly seeking round-the-clock renewable energy supply, not only to meet their sustainability commitments but also to manage their electricity costs.

“Many of them are aiming for 24/7 renewables, which means that every single hour of the day, I want to be powered by 100% renewables. Many of them, yes, they are willing to consume solar power during the day, but they also want to have visibility on what are going to be their costs for power at night, in the early morning when the sun is not shining,” he says.

Securing round-the-clock supply, he says, allows operators to guard against swings in electricity prices when solar power is not available.

Reina says Malaysia has a relatively advanced regulatory framework for renewable energy compared with other countries in the region, but needs to be more ambitious in adding capacity.

Malaysia has historically added about 1GW of solar capacity a year, a rate Reina believes can be raised to meet future demand. The pace of renewable energy growth remains a concern, however, as most of the recent increase in electricity generation has come from fossil fuels.

According to Reina’s presentation, Malaysia’s electricity generation rose by 7.9 terawatt-hours (TWh), or 4.3%, in the 12 months to May 2026. Fossil fuels made up 92% of that increase, adding 7.3TWh, while hydro, solar and bioenergy together added just 0.6TWh.

Natural gas contributed the most at 5TWh, followed by other fossil fuels at 1.4TWh and coal at 0.9TWh.

On the policy front, Fiaz says the government has introduced a requirement for data centres to source at least 30% of their electricity from renewable sources, which creates more demand for solar generation and battery storage.

Citing estimates, he says applying the requirement to new projects could create demand for about 9GW of solar capacity and 4.5GW of battery storage, a market potentially worth RM36 billion.

Whether that demand turns into actual investment, however, depends on how quickly renewable energy projects can be built and connected to the grid.

The discussion also turns to who should pay for this expansion in renewable energy supply, with Reina arguing that large technology companies, particularly hyperscalers, can afford to pay a premium for reliable and cleaner electricity rather than rely entirely on existing infrastructure.

“They will not go out and say, ‘Hey, just charge me.’ But the truth is it’s much more expensive for them to not be able to build a lot of this infrastructure, or to have a data centre built and waiting for a connection, than to pay a premium for the energy or the green technology,” he says.

He says some companies are already taking a more direct role in securing their energy supply by building substations and power plants on site, while also taking care to keep public support by not passing extra costs on to other electricity consumers.

Looking abroad, Fiaz points to Singapore’s approach of allocating data centre capacity based on sustainability considerations, as well as Ireland’s efforts to link new data centre developments with additional power generation.

He also cites Google’s recent investment in water infrastructure in Malaysia as an example of how large investors can help build facilities that serve both industry and local communities.

However, he cautions that having policies and targets is not enough if there is no accurate way to measure whether they are being implemented.

His own research, which tracks 1,000 Malaysian-listed companies from 2018 to 2023, finds that only about 300 regularly report their carbon emissions, even though sustainability reporting is compulsory for publicly listed companies.

He argues that the same principle should apply to data centre investments and the energy infrastructure behind them, with progress judged by measurable results rather than by approvals and plans alone.

stories.title: Equinix opens sixth Singapore data center primed for AI workloads
stories.summary: Equinix has launched its sixth facility in Singapore, specifically engineered to support high-density AI workloads with advanced liquid cooling capabilities. The new data center adds to the company's existing footprint of over 240 facilities globally as it capitalizes on surging enterprise demand for AI infrastructure across Southeast Asia.
stories.why_it_matters: Singapore's tight moratorium on new data center approvals has made each new facility politically and commercially significant. Equinix securing its sixth site signals that incumbents with established relationships and sustainability credentials can still expand in one of the world's most supply-constrained markets, while newer entrants face higher barriers. This deepens the competitive moat for established players and may accelerate AI workload concentration among hyperscale-ready operators.
stories.title_zh: Equinix 启用第六座新加坡数据中心，专为 AI 负载设计
stories.summary_zh: Equinix在新加坡开设了第六座数据中心，专为支持高密度AI工作负载而设计，配备先进的液冷能力。该新设施使该公司在全球超过240座设施的网络得以扩展，因其把握东南亚企业对AI基础设施激增的需求。
stories.why_zh: 新加坡对新数据中心审批的严格限制使每一座新设施在政治和商业层面都具有重要意义。Equinix成功获得第六个站点表明，拥有既有关系和可持续发展资质的incumbent仍可在全球供应最受限的市场之一扩张，而新进入者面临更高壁垒。这加深了已有玩家的竞争护城河，并可能加速AI工作负载向具备hyperscale能力的运营商集中。
stories.content:
Equinix, the digital infrastructure company, announced the opening of its latest data center in Singapore, designed to support artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, and data-intensive workloads. The data center is among the first developed under Singapore’s Data Centre Call for Application framework.

SG6 is Equinix’s sixth International Business Exchange data center in Singapore, according to an Equinix press release, expanding the company’s data center footprint to more than 280 facilities worldwide. G6 is built for high-density AI deployments, with advanced cooling that accommodates power-intensive GPU infrastructure.

“Asia-Pacific is at the forefront of digital transformation, with AI adoption, cloud expansion and data-intensive workloads driving unprecedented demand for high-performance digital infrastructure,” said Cyrus Adaggra, Equinix President of Asia-Pacific. “SG6 strengthens our ability to support customers as they scale across Asia-Pacific, providing the resilient, interconnected and sustainable infrastructure they need to accelerate innovation and capture new growth opportunities.”

Equinix has committed an initial investment of approximately US$ 290 million to SG6. The first phase has 8 MW of capacity, with 20 MW targeted at full buildout. The facility is designed to achieve a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.2 and is targeting Green Mark Platinum certification. Platinum is the highest tier of the Green Mark scheme run by Singapore’s Building and Construction Authority, which has specific criteria for data centers

The facility incorporates rooftop and facade solar photovoltaic systems, rainwater harvesting capabilities, and lower-embodied-carbon construction materials to support more efficient operations.

“Equinix has been investing in Singapore for nearly 25 years, and our new facility will further expand our presence as the neutral exchange where enterprises connect to the clouds, networks and partners they need to innovate and grow. Singapore is one of our most important markets globally, and our continued investment here is a testament to the central role it plays in the digital economy,” said Adaire Fox-Martin, Equinix Chief Executive Officer and President.

The company also said it intends to open a Co-Innovation Facility with the National University of Singapore at the data center. The Co-Innovation Facility will seek to advance technologies that improve data center sustainability and energy efficiency.

Last week, Equinix raised its full-year guidance for the third consecutive quarter. As w.media reported, the company executed more than 25,000 transactions across over 3,200 customers, aiding in delivery of double-digit growth across key metrics. Equinix said that on the back of a record quarter, it expects to deliver revenue between US$ 10.325 billion and US$ 10.365 billion for the full year, up from between US$ 10.205 billion and US$ 10.285 billion as previously guided.

stories.title: OpenAI announces changes to how it handles data centres amid outcry after US midterms
stories.summary: The ChatGPT creator will ensure residents do not pay for the electricity to power those projects

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.title_zh: OpenAI 宣布改变其处理 data centres 的方式，此前因美国中期选举引发抗议
stories.content:
The ChatGPT creator will ensure residents do not pay for the electricity to power those projects

\[SEATTLE\] OpenAI said it will avoid non-disclosure agreements when it negotiates data centre deals and ensure residents do not pay for the electricity to power those projects.

This is part of a framework the company believes should be adopted into laws governing the expansion of artificial intelligence. The series of commitments was released on Thursday (Nov 5).

In a so-called National Community Compact, the company pledges to provide clear data about the potential community impacts of issues including noise, water and energy use.

OpenAI also promised to reduce power usage during peak times, send electricity back to the grid and set local hiring goals, assuming the local workforce allows for it. The AI lab will also publicly report on its progress towards keeping these commitments.

“Households shouldn’t bear the costs of powering data centres,” OpenAI said in the policy document. “Instead, compute campus investment should help expand and modernise America’s energy grid, strengthen reliability, and deliver broader benefits to consumers.”

OpenAI said it had planned the announcement prior to the election returns and has been working on it for months.

It combines some measures the AI research lab has already announced in its data centre projects in areas such as Georgia and adds others that stem from conversations with residents and officials in Georgia, Ohio, Texas and other states, said OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane.

“Certainly a number of them are places that have been particularly impacted by the globalisation of the last 20, 30 years, and for a lot of really good reasons these folks have been really burned by companies and others in the past,” Lehane said.

Voters across the US gave the data centre boom a clear thumbs down on Tuesday night. Gina Hinojosa, who was elected as the first Democratic governor in Texas in more than three decades, has called for an immediate moratorium on data centre development.

Other Democratic gubernatorial victories from Georgia to Ohio and Pennsylvania could leave half of proposed AI data centre additions across the US vulnerable to stricter local scrutiny and pushback.

At least 45 projects valued at US$68 billion were disrupted in some fashion by local opposition in the second quarter of 2026, according to Data Center Watch, a research group.

With data centres becoming increasingly politically unpopular, it is possible some OpenAI projects will be delayed, Lehane said.

“The scale that we are building at there is just going to be a lot of types of things, questions at different levels, state level, local level, that you have to address,” he said. “People are certainly going to be mindful of how voters express themselves.”

OpenAI has been speaking with candidates – incumbents and challengers – over the past few months to share many of its ideas about how to make data centres beneficial to residents, Lehane said, while declining to specify which candidates.

“If you are going to go into a community and you are going to want to build in that community, you do have to do it with the community and get the community input,” Lehane said.

“The fact that people have expressed themselves at the ballot box in the way that they have, is an important message that people have to listen to and react to and respond to. This is how democracy is supposed to work.” BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang drops from world's top 10 richest after chips sell-off
stories.summary: Other big losers included SpaceX’s Elon Musk and Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.title_zh: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang在芯片抛售潮后跌出全球十大富豪榜
stories.content:
Other big losers included SpaceX’s Elon Musk and Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison

JENSEN Huang got an expensive taste of the US Democratic Party’s newfound political power on Thursday (Nov 5).

The Nvidia CEO’s net worth fell by US$15.1 billion to US$150.9 billion as stocks tumbled following Democrats’ sweeping victories in Wednesday’s elections. The loss dropped him to 13th on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index from ninth.

Other big losers were SpaceX’s Elon Musk and Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, who lost US$79.7 billion and US$10.1 billion, respectively.

Expectations that a Democrat-controlled House and Senate will work to constrain construction of data centres – a critical component of AI infrastructure – helped drive shares of semiconductor makers and suppliers of computing power lower.

Nvidia tumbled 9.3 per cent, the most since January 2025, while SpaceX fell 9 per cent and Oracle dropped 6.9 per cent.

All three men, especially Huang, are heavily exposed to the buildout of data centres to support the growing demands of artificial intelligence. Santa Clara, California-based Nvidia is the leading supplier of high-performance computer chips.

Musk’s SpaceX develops its own AI models and constructs data centres to run them, while Ellison’s Oracle has built a big business supplying computing power to others.

The 500 people on the wealth index lost a collective US$185 billion on Thursday, the 14th-biggest one-day rout since Bloomberg began its ranking in 2012.

It comes after a period when tech billionaires were on track for their best year ever, accounting for 36 per cent of the index’s total wealth amid AI’s relentless growth. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Synology sets out Singapore's next step in turning AI ambition into business results
stories.summary: Synology survey: 71.3% of Singapore firms cite data security and privacy as their top AI concern, as it pushes secure, resilient data...
stories.title_zh: Synology阐述新加坡将AI雄心转化为商业成果的下一步
stories.content:
Synology survey: 71.3% of Singapore firms cite data security and privacy as their top AI concern, as it pushes secure, resilient data foundations

Singapore – November 6, 2026 – AI offers businesses new ways to serve customers and improve productivity. Sustaining those benefits requires information that teams can use confidently and systems they can depend on as adoption expands. At Synology Annual Press Event 2026, Synology highlighted the data priorities emerging among Singapore businesses and outlined how it aims to help organizations build a foundation for lasting value from AI. The opportunity is clear in Singapore, where over 90% of respondents to Synology’s survey consider AI-ready infrastructure important to workflow efficiency and productivity. Turning that confidence into results depends on the information businesses can put to work. As AI becomes part of more workflows, the quality and availability of company data, together with the ability to control its use, will shape how successfully organizations can expand adoption. “AI creates value when it helps people do their work better and enables the business to respond more effectively to its customers,” said Antoine Yang, Southeast Asia Head of Synology. “Our focus is to help organizations sustain those gains as adoption grows, with data they can trust and a dependable path to recovery when disruption occurs.”

## Strong data foundation

Turning AI ambitions into reality requires a strong data foundation. However, building this foundation presents significant challenges for businesses. According to the survey, data security and privacy emerged as the most pressing concern among Singapore respondents, cited by 71.3%, followed by data quality and availability at 46.3% and high implementation costs at 41.7%. The findings underscore the need for a secure, accessible, and well-managed data foundation as businesses move from AI ambition to implementation. For business leaders, this means creating the conditions for AI to deliver value consistently across the organization. Teams need reliable information they can access and use within clear rules. Incorporating these requirements into investment planning can help businesses address obstacles to adoption and prepare to extend AI into core operations. These priorities are reflected in where businesses plan to invest. Approximately 58.7% of Singapore respondents prioritize hybrid infrastructure or on premises, compared with just 9.7% prioritizing public cloud. The findings point to a continued need for greater control over business-critical data as organizations prepare for AI. “As businesses expand their data infrastructure, they also need confidence that essential services can recover when disruption occurs,” said Emily Oh, Singapore Country Manager of Synology. While 76% of Singapore respondents express confidence in their ability to recover quickly from ransomware while keeping backup data protected, just 26.9% are very confident. This gap suggests that confidence in recovery remains far from assured. Alongside protecting data and ensuring recovery, businesses also need visibility into how information is used when employees bring AI into their work. In Singapore, nearly 30% of respondents have no visibility into how data submitted to third-party AI tools is handled. This highlights the need for stronger visibility and governance over how business data is shared with and handled by third-party AI tools.

## Top AI priorities for businesses

Drawing on these findings, Synology is focusing on three priorities for businesses embracing AI: scalable data infrastructure, stronger cyber resilience, and productive AI adoption with greater control over business data. Synology’s 2026 data infrastructure launches include PAS7700, its first NVMe SSD storage solution designed for mission-critical workloads, alongside the new-generation FS and RS series, which deliver improved performance over their predecessors for general storage requirements, while Synology Tiering and data reduction on the new DSM 7.4 help organizations use storage more efficiently. To strengthen cyber resilience, Synology ActiveProtect appliances combine dedicated backup infrastructure with centralized management, immutable protection, and automated isolation to help preserve recovery copies when production systems are compromised. The updated operating system, ActiveProtect Manager 2.0, expands workload support to additional enterprise platforms, including Nutanix AHV and Proxmox VE, enabling businesses to protect more of their IT environments through a single platform. Synology is also expanding the ActiveProtect Series with DP5200, a new 1U appliance that gives businesses a compact option for protecting diverse workloads without recurring subscription fees. AI in the workplace rounds out Synology’s 2026 portfolio. Synology Office Suite provides an on-premises foundation for collaboration, with AI assistance for revising documents, creating presentation content, and finding spreadsheet formulas. Synology ChatPlus and Meet extend this collaboration experience to team messaging and online meetings. In physical security, Synology’s DVA7400 surveillance appliance, launched in 2026, applies AI to detection and search to help teams investigate incidents more efficiently. These capabilities allow businesses to apply AI to specific operational needs and assess its value within their own workflows. Looking ahead, Synology also previewed upcoming scale-out storage and hybrid surveillance solutions designed to help enterprises scale their infrastructure as data volumes and operational requirements grow. Together with this year’s launches, these developments reflect Synology’s commitment to providing the secure, resilient, and scalable data foundation businesses need to advance AI adoption with confidence. “When businesses can trust how their data is managed and protected, they are better positioned to turn AI initiatives into lasting business results,” said Oh.

## About Synology

Founded in Taiwan in 2000, Synology is a technology company specializing in network-attached storage (NAS), data backup and recovery, video surveillance, and networking solutions for businesses and individuals worldwide. Over the past two decades, Synology has continuously expanded its ecosystem to help users manage, protect, and unlock the value of data more effectively in the era of cloud, AI, and big data.

stories.title: Caterpillar seeking to expand production of large reciprocating engines and turbines to meet huge data center demand
stories.summary: Caterpillar is looking to expand its production of large reciprocating engines and turbines to meet skyrocketing demand from the data center sector.
stories.title_zh: Caterpillar寻求扩大大型往复式发动机（reciprocating engines）和涡轮机（turbines）生产以满足巨大的数据中心需求
stories.content:
Caterpillar is looking to expand its production of large reciprocating engines and turbines to meet skyrocketing demand from the data center sector.

The heavy machinery manufacturer said it plans to ramp up production during its Q3 earnings call. CEO Joseph Creed said the company reported one of its strongest third-quarter results to date, driven by strong interest from the data center market.

The company reported that its total backlog reached $78 billion, almost double what it was a year ago. It also reported $3.3bn in profit, up 43 percent Year-over-Year (YoY), and $20.7bn in revenue, up 17 percent YoY.

Within its power and energy division, sales totaled $8.8bn, up 18 percent YoY. The majority of this was due to power generation sales, which saw a 30 percent increase from last year, much of which was tied to data center customers.

“We continue to anticipate full-year growth in Power Generation for both Cat reciprocating engines and Solar turbines, driven by increasing energy demand to support the data center build-out related to cloud computing and generative AI,” said Creed.

Creed went on to state that it expects demand to remain strong from the sector, and the company is continuing to do long-term planning with its data center partners.

“We are continuing to do long-term planning with our big data center customers and prime power customers. We are seeing demand for cloud compute and our backup power continue to be strong. And then AI, obviously, comes in on top of that, and the prime power number,” he said.

The company has signed several deals targeting the data center sector in 2026. Most recently, in March, the firm partnered with US microgrid company OnePWR and carbon management firm Vero3 to develop large-scale power generation and carbon storage projects for data centers and other mission-critical facilities.

In January, the company partnered with AI infrastructure developer American Intelligence & Power Corporation (AIP Corp) to supply 2GW of fast-response natural gas generators for AIP’s planned up to 8GW Monarch Compute Campus in Mason County, West Virginia.

Before this, in August of last year, the company partnered with power infrastructure developer Hunt Energy on a multi-year initiative to deliver upwards of 1GW of generation capacity for data centers in North America.
